1000: On my tour they raised a hand at every stop, only to tell me which pieces I had undersold.
1001: I have led this tour a thousand times. One guest knew the prices better than the history.
1002: They joined at the back, moved to the front, and finished the tour giving it.
1003: I pointed to the famous vase. They corrected me on exactly how famous, down to the coin.
1004: Every group has a talker. Mine explained which works were worth stealing, hypothetically.
1005: They asked me to skip the small pieces and linger on the priceless ones. So we lingered.
1006: I said 'follow me, please.' They led instead, pointing out each treasure like a shopping list.
1007: They finished my sentences with numbers I did not want the whole group to hear.
1008: My tour ran long because one guest kept asking the value of everything but the exits.
1009: They thanked me warmly for the tour, then told the group which piece they might come back for someday.
1010: I explained the art. They explained the insurance. The group listened to them.
1011: They corrected my dates twice and my valuations five times, always higher.
1012: Most guests want the story. This one only wanted the receipt.
1013: They stayed behind at one case after the tour, 'to appreciate it properly,' they said.
1014: I have never had a guest grade my tour on which pieces I called priceless.
1015: They asked such precise questions about the locks that I nearly gave a tour of the security.
1016: At the end they tipped me for the tour and the appraisal I never meant to give.
1017: They walked my whole route backward, ending at the priciest piece to ask for a moment alone with it.
1018: I say 'do not touch.' They said 'do not worry,' and I worried.
1019: They knew my script better than I did, and skipped straight to the expensive part.
1020: I know every object in this collection. One guest wanted to know only one thing: its price.
1021: They asked the value of my favorite piece twice, as if the first answer might have grown.
1022: In thirty years no visitor studied one object so hard. By closing they knew it better than I did, and kept it.
1023: They called it the finest thing I had ever catalogued, and this week it is the thing I cannot find.
1024: They asked how I would insure it, how I would move it, how I would miss it. I now know all three.
1025: I explained the object's history. They wrote down only the number at the end.
1026: They came three days running to admire the same piece. On the fourth it admired the exit.
1027: They asked twice what it was worth and never once what it meant.
1028: I have loved that object for decades. They loved it harder in one afternoon.
1029: They wanted to hold it 'to understand its weight.' Now I understand its absence.
1030: They complimented my entire collection, then singled out the one I would never sell.
1031: They asked whether a piece that beautiful could really be priceless, and seemed personally offended.
1032: I keep the catalogue in my head. Today there is a gap exactly the shape of their favorite.
1033: They stood before it so long the guards brought them a chair. I brought nothing; it is gone.
1034: They asked which object I would save first in a fire. I told them. I should not have.
1035: They asked the price twice, sighed both times, and the room has felt emptier ever since.
1036: I described the craftsmanship. They asked only if the number had more zeros.
1037: They said no museum truly deserved a piece that fine. This morning ours no longer has it.
1038: They memorized one object's every detail and none of the rest. Guess which one is missing.
1039: They admired it as if they already owned it, and by dawn the empty shelf agreed.
